237Stiff Person Syndrome and motor mononeuropathy with conduction block: a singular association 
Stiff Person Syndrome and motor mononeuropathy with 
conduction block: A singular association 
S. La Spada, C. Negro, C. Nozzoli, V . De Marco, B. Passarella
Neurosciences Department, BR/1 District Health Centre, Neurology Unit, “A. Perrino” Hospital, Brindisi, Italy
Case report Clin Ter 2006; 157 (3):237-239
Correspondence: Prof. Bruno Passarella  “A. Perrino” Hospital, BR/1 District Health Centre, Neurosciences Department, Neurology Unit, 
72100 Brindisi, Italy; Tel/Fax .0831537317; e-mail enxitp@tin..it
Case report
We report about the case of a 49-year-old housewife, S.P., 
who came to our observation in September 2002. The patient 
had complained, already for two months, of weakness in the 
dorsi-ﬂ exion of the left foot and reported a persistent painful 
contraction involving the abdominal and para-vertebral mu-
scles as well as the proximal muscles of the left lower limb. 
During the clinical examination S.P. showed a slapping gait 
caused by a left foot drop. The patient was also reported to 
have an awkward walking style due to the stiffness affecting 
the extensor and ﬂ exor area of lower limbs - mainly on the 
left side - and of the abdominal and para-vertebral muscles. 
Tendon reﬂ exes and sensibility were normal. The MRI of 
the head was unremarkable and MRI of the spine revealed 
slight lumbar spondylartrhosis. The EMG of the most af-
fected regions reported:
Abstract
The “Stiff person syndrome”(SPS) is a rare dysimmune chronic 
neurological disorder, sometimes paraneoplastic, characterized 
by progressive stiffness, painful persistent or spasmodic muscle 
contractions, mostly involving spine and lower extremities. 
In 60 to 90 percent of cases, non-paraneoplastic forms are 
associated to the presence of anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase 
(anti-GAD) antibodies in the cerebrospinal ﬂ uid and in the serum, 
while anti-amphiphysin antibodies are frequently associated to 
paraneoplastic types. The relevant treatment consists of three basic 
approaches: increase in the inhibitory processes in charge of muscle 
activity control, re-modulation of the immune response, removal 
of any associated neoplasia. Indications regarding the efﬁ cacy of 
high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) also in this dysim-
mune pathology are on the increase.
We described an unusual case of autoimmune SPS associated 
with an exclusively motor left peroneal nerve neuropathy, with 
conduction block, treated with high-dose intravenous immuno-
globulin (IVIG), oral cyclosporine, sodium valproate, baclofen 
and diazepam.
Key words: anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies,
 con-
duction block, intravenous immunoglobulin,  multifocal motor 
neuropathy, stiff person syndrome 
Riassunto 
La “ Sindrome dell’uomo rigido” è una rara patologia neurologica 
cronica, disimmune, caratterizzata da progressiva rigidità, contratture 
muscolari dolorose, persistenti o accessuali, localizzate per lo più a 
livello del tronco  e dei muscoli prossimali degli arti inferiori. In una 
percentuale variabile  dal 60% al 90% dei casi  si è rilevata la presenza 
di Ab anti GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), sia nel liquor che nel 
siero, mentre anticorpi anti amﬁ ﬁ sina sono frequentemente associati 
alla forma paraneoplastica.
Il trattamento terapeutico consiste in tre principali approcci: 
incrementare i processi inibitori nel controllo dell’attività muscolare,

rimodulare la risposta immunitaria, rimuovere, se presente, la neo-
plasia associata. Le indicazioni riguardanti l’efﬁ cacia di alte dosi di 
immunoglobuline i.v.  (IVIG )sono crescenti anche in questa patologia 
disimmune.
Qui descriviamo un insolito caso di SPS autoimmunitaria asso-
ciata ad una neuropatia,esclusivamente motoria, del nervo SPE sx, 
con blocco di conduzione, trattata con IgIV ad alte dosi, ciclosporina 
per os e diazepam.
Parole chiavi: anticorpi anti decarbossilasi dell’acido glutam-
mico, blocco di conduzione, immunoglobuline in vena, neuro-
patia motoria multifocale, sindrome dell’uomo rigido
– a persistent muscle activity despite patient’s attempt to 
reach complete relaxation;
– the temporary interruption of muscle activity upon the 
infusion of intravenous diazepam boles; 
– the lack of mutual inhibition of certain couples of ago-
nist/antagonist muscles (left vastus medialis/ thigh left 
biceps); 
– a motor neuropathy of the left peroneal nerve with motor 
conduction block (Fig. 1) outside of common entrapment 
site (distally to the ﬁ  bula head), with normal sensory 
conduction and absence of F-wave.
– the nervous conduction of the right peroneal nerve, 
right and left median nerves, right and left ulnar nerves 
and right and left posterior tibial nerves was normal by 
examinations (with presence of regular F-waves).  
Laboratory tests reported the signiﬁ  cant presence of 
anti-GAD antibodies in the serum (EIA: 2.000 U. GAD;

positive value>1.050), a moderate normocytic anaemia 
(erythrocytes 3,382,000/ml; Hb 11.8 g/dl), a slight increase 
in the sedimentation rate (1
st hour 24mm; 2 nd hour 47; IK 
23) and an increase in the cerebrospinal ﬂ uid (CSF) proteins 
(51 mg/dl; normal value 0-45) with regular alkaline fractions 
upon CSF isoelectrofocusing. X-ray examinations (chest, 
left knee and coxo-femoral joint), abdominal ultrasound 
scan, electrophysiological testing (SEPs, MEPs, EEG, ECG), 
and further laboratory tests (thyroid functionality, research 
for anti-thyroid/anti-pancreatic islet antibodies, anti-neural 
antibodies, neoplastic markers) performed during her hos-
pitalization were normal.
The initial treatment limited to 10 mg oral diazepam 
three times a day lead to no signiﬁ  cant improvement in 
painful contractions and registered a progressively greater 
weakness in the left-foot dorsi-flexion. Consequently, 
she was again hospitalized in October 2002. Laboratory 
examinations confirmed the anti-GAD (65 and 67 KD 
variants) antibodies in the serum (RIA: 179 U/ml; normal 
value<1 U/ml), and reported the existence of islet cell auto-
antibodies (ICA-IgG:40 UJDF /normal value<5),  tyrosin 
phosphatase IA2 antibodies (16,8 U/ml /normal value<1), 
serum antibodies of IgM class, anti GM1 (1/640; normal 
value<1/640) and anti-sulfatide antibodies (1/16000; nor-
mal value<1/16000). The repetition of EMG conﬁ rmed all 
previous electrophysiological ﬁ ndings, including the motor 
neuropathy of the left peroneal nerve with motor conduction 
block. A total dose of 2 g/kg IVIG was administered over ﬁ ve 
days. Fifteen days later, the dorsi-ﬂ exion of the left foot had 
remarkably improved with the resolution of the conduction 
block (Fig. 2) and a moderate relief for the painful muscle 
contractions. S.P. was discharged with a diagnosis of “stiff 
person syndrome and dysimmune mononeuropathy of the 
left peroneal nerve”. Then, in December 2002 she was di-
agnosed Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1. Baclofen (25 mg per os 
three times a day), tiagabine (5 mg per os three times a day) 
and insulin therapy were added – with gradual increases - to 
the treatment with BDZ (diazepam 10mg per os three times 
a day). In the month of January 2003, the patient received 
4 plasmapheresis treatments. Despite a further increase in 
the doses of administered tiagabine (10mg/three times a 
day) and diazepam (15 mg/three times a day) and two more 
plasmapheresis sessions performed in February 2003, the 
hyperalgic-hypertonic symptomatology got worse, frequently 
triggered by even moderate environmental and emotional 
stimuli. In March 2003 she was diagnosed a Hashimoto’s 
thyroiditis in subclinical hypothyroidism. In the same period 
she began to be treated with immunosuppressants: namely 
with azathioprine, suspended because of liver damage, and 
then with cyclosporine. In May 2003, a CSF control reported 
anti-GAD antibodies in the ﬂ uid at a dosage of 44 units/ml 
(RIA normal value<1). From April 2004, contemporarily 
with the IVIG monthly booster posology increase (from 1 
g/kg to 2 g/kg), spastic-painful events worsened by external 
stimuli, occurring also during previous plasma exchanges, 
had practically disappeared.
To-date, periodic clinical and electrophysiological 
follow-ups no longer reported symptoms or electrophysio-
logical ﬁ ndings of peripheral neuropathy. There occurred 
instead an initial relapsing chronic development of muscle

manifestations with spasmodic painful contractures so resi-
stant to different - even combined - therapeutic approaches 
(with plasmapheresis, azathioprine, diazepam, baclofen, 
anti-epileptic drugs) to cause repeated hospitalizations. Cur-
rent treatment includes oral diazepam (30 mg/day), sodium 
valproate (300 mg/twice a day), cyclosporine (150 mg/day, 
divided into two doses) and baclofen (25 mg/three times a 
day), monthly IVIG booster doses (1g/kg/day for two days), 
associated with substitutive insulin and thyroid therapy. 
The treatment led to improvement of the painful lumbar 
and abdominal muscle contractures so that the patient can 
ambulate independently – however slowly and awkwardly 
– and is able to perform her daily activity, though requiring 
assistance by relatives. 
Fig. 1. Left common peroneal nerve recorded from the extensor digitis 
brevis muscle. Initial  study reported the partial motor conduction 
block (> 50%) outside of common entrapment site.
Fig. 2. Left common peroneal nerve recorded ﬁ  fteen days after the  
administration of a total dose of 2 g/kg IVIG. The study reported the 
resolution of conduction block.

239Stiff Person Syndrome and motor mononeuropathy with conduction block: a singular association 
Discussion
Like many other immuno-mediated diseases, SPS is 
frequently associated with other pathologies having a 
similar pathogenesis (1, 2). Our patient developed mo-
noneuropathy of the left peroneal nerve at the onset of 
symptomatology, Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1, ﬁ  ve months 
later, while Hashimoto’s thyroiditis occurred afterwar-
ds. Literature dealt with no SPS case accompanied by 
autoimmune neuropathies yet. It describes only the case 
of a patient, diabetic for two years, with a moderate non 
immuno-mediated polyneuropathy subsequently found 
as affected with SPS (3). The dysimmune nature of our 
patient’s motor neuropathy, occurring at the onset (before 
diabetes development), was supported by:
– the existence of IgM class anti-GM1 and anti-sulfatide 
antibodies, 
– the optimal response to high-dose IVIG infusions,
– the occurrence of a motor conduction block.
Equating them with forme-fruste or oligosymptomatic 
cases of Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (MMN), Felice (4) 
described three cases of monofocal motor neuropathy without 
anti-GM1 antibodies, with a positive response to IVIG.
The conduction block motor neuropathy, without evi-
dence of sensory damage, associated with described SPS, 
proposed two hypotheses concerning its possible noso-
graphic reference:
1. It might be the onset of an MMN, with typical course 
and multifocal and asymmetrical distribution favorably 
inﬂ uenced by the adopted therapy. IVIGs are indeed 
reported to be the prime therapy with MMN. Monthly 
IVIG infusions and oral cyclosporine reduced – in our 
patient - SPS typical muscle stiffness and pains and also 
probably inhibited the course - chronic, progressive or 
relapsing – of the monofocal conduction block motor 
neuropathy.
2. It may be considered as a particular type of dysimmune 
chronic motor neuropathy with single-phase course, where 
the presence of Anti-GM1 and Anti-sulfatide antibodies 
are the evidence of a widespread immune alteration. 
The diagnosis of multifocal motor neuropathy (5 ) re-
quires, inter alia,  the clinical signiﬁ cance of weakness in 
two or more motor nerves with detectable motor conduction 
blocks outside of common entrapment sites. 
Notwithstanding the existence of descriptions regard-
ing other anecdotal “uncommon” cases of MMN (6, 7) not 
completely matching mentioned criteria, it is not considered 
necessary to resort to a possible widening of diagnostic 
criteria. Instead - also on account of the dysimmune motor 
mononeuropathy we noticed in our patient, S.P., and of the 
efﬁ cacy of the treatment with IVIG – it would be worth 
devoting a growing attention to the identiﬁ cation of “oligo-
symptomatic” or “uncommon” types of neuropathies not 
much recognized - and therefore treated – as yet.
Therapeutically, high-dose IVIG proved also here to be 
well tolerated and efﬁ cacious in the control of SPS typical 
symptomatology (8, 9) and in the remission of left peroneal 
nerve conduction block motor neuropathy. Last thirty years’ 
controlled clinical studies analyzed by Dalakas (10) may 
indicate IVIG as “ﬁ  rst-line” evidence-based therapy for 
Guillaine-Barrè Syndrome (GBS), CIDP and MMN. It is 
a “second-line” therapy in case of SPS, Dermatomyositis 
(DM), Myasthenia Gravis (MG) and Lambert-Eaton My-
asthenic Syndrome (LEMS). For other pathologies, such 
as the paraproteinemic demyelinating polyneuropathies

associated with anti-MAG antibodies and the Inclusion 
Body Myiositis (IBM) they have a statistically insigniﬁ cant 
marginal and variable efﬁ cacy. In our patient IVIG was jus-
tiﬁ ed mainly by the unusual association with the described 
dysimmune motor neuropathy and the scarce efﬁ  cacy of 
other therapies. Only the IVIG monthly infusion (2 g/kg) 
plus oral daily diazepam, cyclosporine, baclofen and sodium 
valproate allowed to remarkably reduce the spasmodic 
painful muscle contracture previously signiﬁ  cantly limit-
ing patient’s autonomy despite the repeated plasmapheresis 
combined with immunosuppressive therapies (azathioprine, 
suspended because of liver damage, and cyclosporine) and 
anti-epileptic drugs, in the attempt to increase the inhibi-
tory processes in motor activity control (sodium valproate 
and vigabatrin).

3. Goppert D, Gardill K, Beischer W, et al.: The stiff-man

6. Maurer M, Stoll G, Toyka KV: Multifocal motor neuropathy

7. Vucic S, Dawson K, Sun D, et al.: Pure motor mononeuro-

of multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block. Clin

8. Dalakas MC, Fujii M, Li M, et al.: High-Dose intravenous
